definition: the range of tasks someone has been given
hook: Mainly British: what you've been sent to do.

examples.interview: My remit was narrow: build the model, not make the recommendation.
examples.finance: The fund's remit is to invest only in green infrastructure.
examples.everyday: Planning the playlist is outside my remit.

weak.sentence: My job was only just to build the model.

definition: something that leads or signals a wider trend
hook: The lead sheep (a wether) wore a bell, and the flock followed it.

examples.interview: I follow FedEx's earnings because it's a bellwether for global trade.
examples.finance: Semiconductor stocks are often a bellwether for the broader tech sector.
examples.everyday: That county is a bellwether in presidential elections.

weak.sentence: FedEx's earnings are a good sign of what's coming for global trade.
weak.phrase: a good sign of what's coming

definition: careful to consider risks before acting or speaking
hook: Latin for "looking around": you look around before you move.

examples.interview: I was circumspect about sharing projections until the numbers were final.
examples.finance: Lenders have become more circumspect about commercial real estate.
examples.everyday: Be circumspect about what you post online during recruiting.

weak.sentence: Lenders have gotten a lot more careful about commercial real estate.

definition: clear, logical, and convincing
hook: Related to "cogitate," to think hard: a cogent argument is well thought out.

examples.interview: She made a cogent case for exiting the position before earnings.
examples.finance: The memo laid out a cogent thesis in two pages.
examples.everyday: That's a cogent argument for leaving an hour earlier.

weak.sentence: She made a really convincing case for selling before earnings.

definition: reducing earnings per share or ownership percentage
hook: Adding water dilutes a drink; issuing shares dilutes owners.

examples.interview: Issuing new shares would be dilutive, so I'd fund the deal with debt.
examples.finance: The stock fell because the offering was dilutive.
examples.everyday: Adding more people to the project was dilutive to my grade.

weak.sentence: Issuing shares would make each share worth less of the earnings.
weak.phrase: make each share worth less of the earnings

definition: by which; through which
hook: Where plus by: the way something happens.

examples.interview: I set up a system whereby each member reviewed one model a week.
examples.finance: The deal includes an earnout whereby the sellers get paid more if targets are hit.
examples.everyday: We have an agreement whereby whoever cooks doesn't clean.

weak.sentence: I set up a system where, like, each member reviewed one model.

definition: to the extent that
hook: In so far as: only as far as this goes.

examples.interview: The plan works insofar as the sponsors renew, so I built a backup.
examples.finance: Stocks benefit insofar as rate cuts boost earnings.
examples.everyday: I'm ready for the test insofar as I've done the readings.

weak.sentence: The plan works only as long as and to the degree the sponsors renew.
weak.phrase: only as long as and to the degree

definition: specific to one person or thing; peculiar to it
hook: From Greek idios, "one's own." In finance, idiosyncratic risk is risk that belongs to one company, not the whole market.

examples.interview: The drop was idiosyncratic to the company, not a sector-wide problem.
examples.finance: Diversification reduces idiosyncratic risk but not market risk.
examples.everyday: He has an idiosyncratic way of organizing his notes.

weak.sentence: The drop was just a thing specific to that one company.

definition: the most important part that holds everything together
hook: The pin that keeps a wheel on its axle.

examples.interview: Our treasurer was the linchpin of the club, so I documented everything she did.
examples.finance: The patent is the linchpin of the company's valuation.
examples.everyday: Coffee is the linchpin of my morning.

weak.sentence: Our treasurer was the key piece holding it all together.
weak.phrase: key piece holding it all together

definition: apparently or supposedly, though maybe not really
hook: From Latin ostendere, "to show": what's shown on the surface.

examples.interview: The reorganization was ostensibly about efficiency, but it was really about cutting costs.
examples.finance: The buyback was ostensibly to return capital, but it also lifted earnings per share.
examples.everyday: He came over, ostensibly to study, but mostly to eat.

weak.sentence: The reorg was supposedly about efficiency, I guess.

definition: something hanging over a stock or market that holds it back, like a big pending sale
hook: Like a rock ledge hanging overhead: a looming threat.

examples.interview: The lawsuit is an overhang on the stock until it's resolved.
examples.finance: The founder's planned share sale created an overhang.
examples.everyday: The unfinished paper was an overhang on my whole weekend.

weak.sentence: The lawsuit is a thing holding the stock back.
weak.phrase: a thing holding the stock back

definition: in spite of
hook: Literally "not standing in the way."

examples.interview: Notwithstanding the weak quarter, I think the long-term thesis holds.
examples.finance: Notwithstanding higher rates, housing demand stayed firm.
examples.everyday: Notwithstanding the rain, the game went on.

weak.sentence: Even with the weak quarter and everything, the thesis holds.
weak.phrase: Even with the weak quarter and everything

definition: impossible to keep defending or keep going
hook: From Latin tenere, "to hold": a position you can't hold.

examples.interview: Running the club on volunteer hours alone became untenable, so I proposed paid roles.
examples.finance: The debt load became untenable once rates rose.
examples.everyday: Sharing one bathroom with five people was untenable.

weak.sentence: Running it on volunteers alone just wasn't working anymore.

definition: adding to earnings per share or value
hook: From Latin accrescere, "to grow," as in accrue.

examples.interview: The deal is accretive to earnings in year one, which helps sell it to shareholders.
examples.finance: Management said the acquisition would be immediately accretive.
examples.everyday: Every practice is accretive to my skills, even the bad ones.

weak.sentence: The deal makes earnings per share go up in year one.
weak.phrase: makes earnings per share go up

definition: the area someone is responsible for or has authority over
hook: What falls within your view.

examples.interview: Sponsorships were outside my purview, so I connected the vendor with our treasurer.
examples.finance: Antitrust review falls under the regulator's purview.
examples.everyday: Grocery shopping is my roommate's purview.

weak.sentence: Sponsorships weren't really my area to handle.

definition: more than is needed; unnecessary
hook: From Latin, "overflowing": the extra that spills over.

examples.interview: I cut superfluous slides so the pitch fit in ten minutes.
examples.finance: The merger eliminated superfluous layers of management.
examples.everyday: The second charger was superfluous.

weak.sentence: I cut the extra unneeded slides to fit ten minutes.

definition: in finance, a long-term trend that lasts many years, beyond normal cycles
hook: From Latin saeculum, "an age": a trend measured in decades, not quarters.

examples.interview: Cloud adoption is a secular trend, so a weak quarter doesn't change my thesis.
examples.finance: Some economists think we've entered a secular period of higher rates.
examples.everyday: Remote work looks like a secular shift, not a phase.

weak.sentence: Cloud adoption is a really long-lasting trend.

definition: for the next small change, rather than overall
hook: Economics thinks at the margin: what happens with one more unit?

examples.interview: At the margin, another hire won't speed things up much; we need better tools.
examples.finance: At the margin, buyers are getting more price-sensitive.
examples.everyday: At the margin, one more hour of studying isn't worth losing sleep.

weak.sentence: Adding just one more extra hire won't speed things up much.
weak.phrase: Adding just one more extra hire

definition: when investors give up and sell in a panic, often near a bottom
hook: Military surrender: the army capitulates.

examples.interview: The volume spike looked like capitulation, so I started building a position.
examples.finance: Some traders wait for capitulation before buying a falling stock.
examples.everyday: My capitulation came at 2am when I finally ordered pizza.

weak.sentence: The selloff looked like everyone finally giving up and selling.
weak.phrase: everyone finally giving up and selling

definition: a disruption that pushes prices away from where they normally should be
hook: Like a dislocated shoulder: something knocked out of its normal place.

examples.interview: Distressed debt funds look for market dislocations to buy assets cheaply.
examples.finance: The pandemic caused a dislocation in the Treasury market.
examples.everyday: Moving mid-semester caused some dislocation in my routine.

weak.sentence: Funds look for moments of market chaos and weirdness to buy cheap.

definition: a turning point after which things are very different
hook: A ridge where rain flows one way or the other.

examples.interview: Leading my first live deal was a watershed moment for my confidence.
examples.finance: The 2008 crisis was a watershed for bank regulation.
examples.everyday: Getting my license was a watershed in my independence.

weak.sentence: My first deal was a really big turning point moment.

definition: in proportion to something else
hook: "Co" plus "measure": two things measured together.

examples.interview: I spent time on each issue commensurate with its impact on the deal.
examples.finance: Investors demand returns commensurate with the risk they take.
examples.everyday: The price was commensurate with the quality.

weak.sentence: Investors want returns that match up with the risk they take.
